decision_reason: A1's closest unseen pair, sitting and standing, differs only in posture_inclination. The unspecified placement within each leg does not justify adding a reliably observable seated knee or hip configuration. Likewise, distinguishing stepper from cross trainer through obligatory arm motion would assume an unspecified exercise technique. Preserve these uncertain contrasts rather than manufacture separability. Add one supported static-orientation distinction: torso_lateral_tilt separates the nearly identical lying anchors by gravity-relative torso geometry instead of relying on their questionable smoothness difference. This improves the semantic description of the static seen anchors used by sitting and standing, but does not claim to resolve that unseen pair or improve recognition performance. Preserve the existing movement dimensions supporting stair, walking and stepper transfer.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or rotational motion during the activity.

attributes.name: translational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained linear progression or locomotor translation within a window.

levels.High: Prominent sustained translational or locomotor motion.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: torso_lateral_tilt
attributes.definition: Degree to which the torso's anatomical left-right direction aligns with gravity, distinguishing lateral torso tilt from forward or backward inclination.

levels.Low: The torso's left-right direction is nearly perpendicular to gravity, with little lateral tilt.
levels.Medium: The torso's left-right direction is oblique to gravity, indicating moderate lateral tilt.
levels.High: The torso's left-right direction is nearly aligned with gravity, indicating a predominantly side-on torso orientation.

operations.reason: motion_intensity: G3 supports overall acceleration and rotation magnitude across the available body sensors. Retain the exertion-related contrast linking ascending stairs with inclined treadmill walking and stepper with cross trainer. Pace and technique can change magnitude, so intensity alone should not define these distinctions.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in 15 deg inclined positions)

operations.reason: cadence: G6 supports repetition rate through recurring acceleration and rotation. It transfers periodic movement structure from treadmill and cycling activities to walking, stairs and stepper without presuming particular speeds. Harmonics, alternating limbs and self-selected pace can make the repetition unit or ordinal boundary ambiguous.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)
cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: smoothness: G9 supports sustained rapid fluctuations in the available motion signals. Retain continuous-versus-jarring movement semantics for stepper and stair descent, with cross trainer and jumping as transferable anchors. Speed and sensor attachment affect fluctuations; the supplied back-versus-side lying difference is not a dependable physical contrast.

impulsiveness: G10 supports isolated abrupt changes transmitted through leg and torso acceleration. Retain landing-related evidence connecting descending stairs with jumping and separating it from supported continuous exercise. Footwear, landing strategy and attachment can attenuate peaks; impact magnitude does not establish vertical travel direction.

posture_inclination: G1 supports gravity-relative mean orientation across torso and leg sensors. Retain the existing static-posture distinction and inclined-motion transfer. Global load-bearing configuration is not identical to torso orientation: upright sitting, individual lean and unspecified leg placement can blur interpretation. Do not assume that sitting always produces an intermediate torso angle.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in 15 deg inclined positions)

operations.reason: posture_variability: G12 supports temporal changes of gravity-relative orientation, particularly at the torso. Retain the distinction between relatively fixed exercise posture and changing locomotor configuration, using treadmill walking and rowing as anchors. Local limb swings and dynamic acceleration can mimic global posture changes and must not be interpreted as equivalent.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: rotational_motion: G2 supports sustained angular motion in torso, arm and leg gyroscopes. Preserve limb-rotation structure shared by stepper, cross trainer and cycling. Rotation amplitude depends on technique and movement range; high rotation does not imply whole-body turning or independently distinguish the exercise machines.
seen_anchors: cycling on an exercise bike in vertical positions

operations.reason: translational_motion: G13 supports short-window translational-motion proxies. Preserve the semantic distinction between progressing locomotion and stationary exercise, using treadmill and elevator movement as partial anchors. Constant velocity, drift and moving supports limit observability: these signals do not establish absolute displacement, floor changes or reliable outdoor-versus-treadmill separation.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: motion_regularity: G11 and G6 support recurrence and consistency of movement timing. Retain structured exercise versus less constrained movement as a transferable distinction for parking-lot walking and stepper. Uninterrupted outdoor walking can be highly regular, and static signals can also be predictable; regularity is neither environment identity nor cadence.
seen_anchors: walking on a treadmill with a speed of 4 km/h (in flat)

operations.reason: torso_lateral_tilt: G1 supports the gravity-relative lateral orientation of the torso sensor. Side lying aligns the anatomical left-right torso direction with gravity, whereas back lying and ordinary upright postures do not. This adds a stable, independent distinction between the two close lying anchors used for static unseen activities, without pretending to separate sitting from standing. Predictability requires a consistent or known sensor-to-torso orientation; mounting rotation, lateral leaning and transitions introduce ambiguity. No such alignment is assumed to have been verified.

semantic_redundancy_review: The ten attributes retain distinct physical meanings. Intensity describes magnitude; cadence describes repetition rate; regularity describes consistency. Smoothness concerns sustained rapid changes, whereas impulsiveness concerns brief peaks. Posture inclination describes global uprightness, posture variability describes its temporal change, and torso lateral tilt describes a directional component of static torso orientation: back and side lying can share global inclination while differing in lateral tilt. Rotation and translation remain distinct, although translation has important inertial-observability limitations. No redundant arm-involvement, elevation-direction or joint-flexion dimension is added because the supplied semantics and sensor placement do not establish sufficiently stable evidence. Existing A1 prototype assignments are not revised or endorsed as measured sensor differences.
